tier1.text: Each knee joint works mainly as a hinge, letting the leg bend and straighten. Three bones form each knee joint: the thighbone (femur), the shinbone (tibia) and the kneecap (patella). Between the femur and tibia sit two cartilage pads called menisci, which cushion the bones. Strong bands called ligaments span between the bones and support the knee, especially when it is straight.

tier2.text: Each knee joint works mainly as a hinge, letting the leg bend and straighten. The knee joint is the body's largest joint. Three bones form each knee joint: the thighbone (femur), the shinbone (tibia) and the kneecap (patella). As the knee bends and straightens, the femur rolls and glides on the tibia, keeping the two bones in stable contact. When the knee straightens fully, a slight rotation of the femur locks the knee into the most stable position for bearing weight. Between the femur and tibia sit two cartilage pads called menisci, which provide padding and improve the fit between the two bones. The knee's ligaments, strong bands spanning between bones, include a collateral ligament on each side and two cruciate ligaments inside the joint. The anterior cruciate ligament resists hyperextension, or straightening too far, while the posterior cruciate ligament keeps the femur from sliding forward when the bent knee bears weight. The patella sits inside the tendon of the quadriceps femoris, the large muscle at the front of the thigh, and protects that tendon from friction against the femur. The quadriceps femoris muscle group straightens the leg at the knee, while the opposing hamstrings bend the leg.
